subject: Computer Networking
title: Network Interface Cards
description: A quick win: understand Network Interface Cards.

hook.text: Every networked device needs a NIC — the hardware that speaks the network's language.

buildup.text: A NIC frames data into packets, manages transmission timing, and detects errors on the wire.

discovery.text: Every NIC has a unique MAC address — a 48-bit hardware ID burned in at the factory. No two match.

twist.text: Modern NICs are built into motherboards. Dedicated cards now mainly serve servers needing extra speed.

climax.text: Some NICs offload checksums, encryption, or TCP from the CPU to boost performance.

punchline.text: The NIC is your device's passport to the network.

quiz.question: What unique identifier does every NIC have?
options: A MAC address assigned at the factory
An IP address from the ISP
A serial number from the operating system

details.summary: A network interface card connects a computer to a network by converting data into electrical or optical signals for transmission. Modern NICs handle speeds from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps and offload tasks like checksum calculation and TCP segmentation from the CPU.
details.whyItMatters: The NIC is the physical gateway between a computer and the network. NIC capabilities directly affect throughput, latency, and CPU overhead for network-intensive applications.
takeaways: NICs convert data between computer buses and network signals
Hardware offloading reduces CPU load for network processing
Server NICs support speeds from 10 Gbps to 100 Gbps

faq.question: What is NIC hardware offloading?
faq.answer: Hardware offloading moves network processing tasks from the CPU to the NIC itself. Common offloads include TCP checksum calculation, segmentation, and receive-side scaling. This frees CPU cycles for application work and is critical for high-throughput servers.

faq.question: Do modern computers still have separate NICs?
faq.answer: Most laptops and desktops have NICs built into the motherboard. Servers and high-performance workstations use add-in PCIe NICs for faster speeds, multiple ports, or advanced features like RDMA. Data center servers commonly use 25 Gbps or 100 Gbps add-in cards.
